body_markdown:
One minute you’re sitting on a balcony in South Beach, taking in the views. The next, you’re rummaging through a haul of recently acquired Soviet car parts. That’s Miami, baby. And no visit to South Florida is complete without a visit to Zakharov Auto Parts in Hialeah.


Is it strange for a Miami storefront to trade in Soviet-era machinery? Seems like a lot of overhead and infrastructure just to sell to weirdos like myself. Well, apparently sales are not the primary goal. (Though they did sell me some goodies.) Zakharov Auto Parts is a vital *shipping* conduit, bringing in parts from Eastern Europe that eventually find their way into Cuba. There are still a lot of Cubans who drive Lada, Moskvich, Aleko, Volga, and UAZ vehicles for daily transportation.


Cuban traffic, pseudo-frozen in time, is a record of the country’s history. After the 1959 revolution and the American embargo that followed, the flow of new Detroit iron stopped cold. Soviet-bloc cars didn’t arrive in real numbers until Cuba joined the Soviet economic organization[COMECON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comecon) in 1972. From then on, Ladas, Moskvich 412s and 2140s, Volgas, and UAZ off-roaders were allocated by the state, often as rewards to workers, professionals, and officials, rather than sold outright. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the supply of new cars and factory parts dried up overnight. Cubans have been keeping these cars alive with ingenuity and imported spares ever since. That’s where places like Zakharov come in.


Extremely fast and helpful staff.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I heard about this place a few years ago. It seemed like a mythical place, a shop that might not even exist by the time I got down to Miami, one day. Not the case. I was in town for a NASCAR banquet. Shortly after breakfast, I broke off from my group, stole the rental car, and headed inland a bit. I had at least two hours before I needed to press my suit for the evening; might as well spend that time scrounging through cross-reference guides for Moskvich cars and practicing my Spanish.


As I approached the building, situated between a restaurant supply store and a vape shop, Soviet car iconography immediately jumped out at me. I mean, hell, a Lada cylinder head and pictures of UAZ, Moskvich, and Volga models are displayed right on the front windows. A very secure-looking door stood between me and a confusing array of car parts.


The Moskvich wall.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


From the moment I walked inside, I think it was obvious to everyone there that I wasn’t the typical client. For starters, I had to unearth all my high school Spanish on the spot. Pen and paper came in handy for scribbling down engine numbers, models, and part names. The proprietor, however, didn’t know what to do with me. Eventually, showing him some photos on my phone convinced him that I actually own a Moskvich, have owned Ladas, and so on.


My Moskvich 407 was a bit of a mystery to him, as was its biggest cross-reference parts friend, the 408. After all, Cuba didn’t join COMECON until 1972, long after the 407 was out of production and with the 408 nearing the end of its run. Nevertheless, I was accepted at long last as a serious buyer.


The Volga department. Please enjoy your browsing.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Digging through my phone further, I found a photo of the Moskvich 412 engine and transmission I had brought back from Germany, which I’ve been meaning to get running. Even if I couldn’t find any 407 parts, surely snagging a few 412 parts was some sort of progress. And becoming a paying client ingratiated me with the staff at Zakharov.


The store walls were lined with glass cabinets and wire racks, each subdivided into Volga, Moskvich, Lada, UAZ, and other makes I couldn’t readily identify. I even noticed a few Peugeot parts, spotting some XUD diesel components and 405 marker lights. Having confessed that I’d owned about half of the cars in the building already, I didn’t want to stretch my credibility by getting into my Peugeot and French car ties at that moment, so we focused on Moskvich stuff.


That’s a lotta Lada.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I had already gone through my car’s braking system and rebuilt everything years ago, back when I was living in Germany, so luckily I didn’t need much in the stopping department. The 407’s overlap with the later 412 and 2140 is pretty slim in this area, anyway. Instead, I focused on ignition components, turning up a distributor cap that I believe will fit either application. As I browsed, the proprietor kept bringing out more parts from behind the counter to see if I could use them. I graciously accepted most of them, feeling somewhat under the gun because, surprisingly, I wasn’t the only one in the shop, and the customer service was curt. I endeavored to move quickly, clocking that this wasn’t a place to sit around and linger. Relying on my internal cross-reference guide of sh**box car parts, and my memory of what I might need, I started pointing at things on the shelves. *Carburetor rebuild kit for a 2140* , check. *Oil pan gasket for the UZAM-412* , check. *Exhaust flange gasket for UZAM-412* , check.


Whether due to the language barrier or availability, I wasn’t able to fill my cart with everything I hoped for. A set of pistons and rings and a gasket set for the UZAM-412 were high on my wish list, as well as a distributor rotor for the 408. Oh well… random beggar tourists can’t be choosers.


I was able to chat with the owner, briefly, about the shop’s business model. Oftentimes, it turns out, people heading down to visit family in Cuba buy parts to carry in their suitcases, limited to an extent by Cuba’s personal import limits. Anything over those limits now gets hit with duties (payable in U.S. dollars) rather than confiscated outright, but Cuban customs inspects nearly every bag. So it pays to pack carefully.


A carb kit for the UZAM-412 on the shop floor.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


For everything else that needs transport, there’s one word, emblazoned across the front of the building: “[envíos](https://www.spanishdict.com/translate/env%C3%ADos) .” Shipments make their way to Cuba by air or sea freight; car parts clear Cuban customs on arrival.


I was a little nervous about bringing my full bag up to the register, but it came to a more than fair price: $80 for everything. Not to mention the hearty offer they gave me to order whatever parts I might need from former Soviet republics. These days, that’s huge.


Well, two hours gone. After that, it was time to act like a normal professional person again and press my suit. And, of course, send photos to all of my car friends who would never otherwise believe there is a Soviet car part and shipping emporium in less than 15 miles from South Beach.


I told the nice man that I had several grills already… just no car.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)
